v: One of the worst movies I had seen after Brahmotsavam — a short-film-sized story stretched endlessly in the name of realism until patience itself becomes the real victim.
e: Falaknuma Das has a few actors doing genuinely good work, but their effort disappears inside a 150-minute film that felt painfully stretched and repetitive. I am normally open to realistic cinema, but here the refusal to use emotion, twists or entertainment made the so-called realism feel more like a test of patience than a strength.
body:
One of the worst movies I had seen after Brahmotsavam!!!!!

The basic storyline felt like something that could comfortably have worked as a twenty-minute short film.

Instead, it is stretched… stretched… and stretched into roughly 150 minutes.

For me, Falaknuma Das became an example of how badly an audience’s patience can be tested when a filmmaker becomes so committed to a so-called realistic approach that he refuses almost every bit of cinematic liberty.

There is barely any attempt to build stronger emotion, twists or entertainment around the story.

A few actors perform very well, and that deserves acknowledgment.

Unfortunately, their efforts are wasted because we keep returning to the same far-stretched, repetitive scenes without enough purpose or progression.

I am generally open to different genres and to realistic films.

So my problem is not realism itself.

The problem is that here I could see almost nothing beyond the director’s determination to make a realistic film with a realistic story, realistic emotions and realistic dialogues — even when that realism was doing very little to keep the movie engaging.

For a normal moviegoer, this can become extremely frustrating.

For me, it was a total waste of time!!!!!

v: REEListic story dealt with REAListic emotions! A must-watch for emotional-content lovers, with Nani making an award-worthy role look like a cakewalk and the cricket portions landing beautifully.
e: Jersey is unapologetically emotional rather than mass entertainment, so its impact depends heavily on what kind of cinema you enjoy. For viewers who connect with realistic drama, Nani’s effortless performance, Gowtam Tinnanuri’s direction, well-shot cricket scenes and touching dialogues make it a deeply rewarding watch.
body:
REEListic story dealt with REAListic emotions!!!!

If you are a fan of movies driven by emotional content, Jersey is a must watch.

If you are a regular movie lover, it is still worth a one-time watch.

And if you watch cinema purely for mass entertainment, then this may simply not be your kind of film.

What could have become an award-winning, once-in-a-lifetime performance for many actors feels almost like a cakewalk for Nani.

He makes the frustration, vulnerability and determination of the character feel completely natural.

Director Gowtam Tinnanuri does full justice to the emotional theme, and the cricket portions are also shot really well.

The songs themselves are fairly ordinary, but the BGM is much better.

It stays relatively subtle and still manages to elevate the emotional mood whenever required.

Shraddha Srinath, Sathyaraj and the little kid all do complete justice to their respective roles.

Special mention also goes to the dialogues.

They often sound conversational rather than manufactured, and several lines carry the pain of the character without needing theatrical presentation.

One of the strongest ideas in the film is that success is not merely about talent; sometimes it is about the ability to keep trying even when everyone around you has quietly stopped expecting anything from you.

That combination of cricket, failure, family and self-respect is what made Jersey work for me.

v: I felt more FRUSTRATION than Fun. The story, silly comedy, songs and overacting exhausted me; the one genuine pleasure is watching vintage Venky return to comedy after a long gap.
e: F2 reminded me of the old family multi-starrers where frustrated husbands run away from domestic life, get into trouble and eventually rediscover the value of family. Anil Ravipudi revives that template with plenty of loud comedy, but almost everything irritated me except Venkatesh slipping comfortably back into his vintage comic zone.
body:
I felt FRUSTRATED more than I felt any Fun!!!!

Back in the late 1990s and early 2000s, there was a phase of so-called family multi-starrers where a group of husbands or friends became fed up with their wives and families, wandered onto the wrong path and eventually realised the importance of marriage and family.

Movies like Sandade Sandadi and Kshemanga Velli Labhanga Randi wrapped that basic idea in endless, often mindless comedy.

They also tended to feature a familiar combination of established or fading stars, struggling younger heroes and dependable comedy performers such as Rajendra Prasad.

Anil Ravipudi seems heavily inspired by that golden era here — only this time he brings together Venkatesh, Varun Tej and, once again, Mr. Rajendra Prasad.

Unfortunately, almost every major ingredient frustrated me.

The story was frustrating.

The silly comedy was frustrating.

The songs and BGM were frustrating.

The family drama was frustrating.

And the heroines and Prakash Raj are pushed into such exaggerated performances that even they became frustrating.

The one genuine FUN for me was watching vintage Venky return to a full comedy movie after a long gap.

His timing still works, and whenever he gets space to play, you get a glimpse of why he was so comfortable in this genre for years.

But that alone was not enough to rescue the movie for me.

v: Boyapati’s regular mass template gets turned past OVER-the-top — family, villain, fights, dialogues and even physics go berserk. Ram Charan is the lone positive, comfortably surviving the madness.
e: Vinaya Vidheya Rama takes every familiar Boyapati ingredient and pushes it several levels beyond excess: more emotion, more villainy, louder dialogues, bigger fights and logic that disappears almost completely. Ram Charan’s ease with the high-voltage material is the only real positive I found, even though my daughter apparently had a very different verdict 😄
body:
Ram Charan did a Balakrishna!!!!!

The regular Boyapati template is easy to recognise: an emotional family, a powerful hero, a cruel villain, high-voltage dialogues, top-class fights… and very weak physics.

But with Ram Charan and a big budget on board, Boyapati appears to have decided that normal excess was simply not enough.

So we get an OVER-emotional family, an OVER-powerful hero, an OVER-cruel villain, OVER-voltage dialogues and completely over-the-top fights.

And somehow the physics becomes even weaker than usual 😄

This time, the film does not stop with physics either.

Biology, geography and basic common sense all appear to receive similar treatment.

While Boyapati is busy pushing those limits, DSP’s music and BGM also disappointed me badly.

The one clear positive in the entire movie is Ram Charan.

He looks completely at ease delivering the high-voltage dialogues and throwing himself into the oversized fight sequences.

His commitment is never the problem.

The material surrounding him is.

For me, the movie becomes so exaggerated that even the usual suspension of disbelief expected from a Boyapati mass entertainer is not enough.

P.S. My daughter LOVED the movie!!!!! 😄
